chapters.title: Chapter 4: Valuing a Business on Its Own Cash Flows

lessons.title: Terminal Value and Why Small Assumptions Move Big Numbers

children.text: In Lesson 4.2, Konkan Ceramics came out at an enterprise value of about ₹245.3 crore. About 73% of that came from one line: the terminal value. Five years of detailed forecasting, argued over line by line, decided roughly a quarter of the answer. A single assumption about the year 2032 onwards decided the rest. This lesson is about that line.

body.text: Terminal value is where most of a DCF's value lives and where most of its dishonesty hides. It is one formula with two inputs, and moving either of them by a percentage point can move the valuation by a quarter.

children.text: Why the Number Exists at All

A business does not stop trading at the end of your forecast. You could forecast fifty years, but nobody believes year 34 of a spreadsheet, and discounting makes those years nearly worthless anyway. So the convention is to forecast in detail for as long as you have real visibility, usually five years, and then collapse everything after that into one figure.

cells: Perpetuity growth, also called Gordon growth
Final year cash flow × (1 + g) ÷ (WACC - g)
The standard in valuation reports, and in most regulatory and reporting work
Exit multiple
Final year EBITDA × an assumed multiple
Common in private equity, where the fund genuinely intends to sell in year five

body.text: Neither method is more correct. The useful trick is to run both and check they agree. If your perpetuity growth assumption implies an exit multiple no buyer would pay, or your exit multiple implies perpetual growth faster than the economy, you have found a problem that no amount of forecasting detail will fix.

children.text: The Perpetuity Formula, Under a Microscope

body.caption: Everything turns on the denominator, which is the gap between the cost of capital and the growth rate

children.text: For Konkan Ceramics, final year free cash flow is ₹23.0 crore and the cost of capital is 12.5%. Change only the growth rate and watch what happens.

body.caption: Konkan Ceramics: terminal value at different growth assumptions (₹ crore)

body.title: Enterprise value at different terminal growth rates

body.text: From 3% to 7% growth, enterprise value moves from about ₹205 crore to about ₹315 crore, roughly half as much again. Nothing about the tiles, the customers or the factory changed. The denominator shrank from 9.5% to 5.5%, and that is the entire story.

body.title: Move the growth rate
body.prompt: Using Konkan Ceramics' final year free cash flow of ₹23.0 crore and a 12.5% cost of capital, what is the terminal value if long-run growth is assumed at 6%? Answer in ₹ crore, to the nearest crore.
body.explanation: ₹23.0 crore × 1.06 ÷ (0.125 - 0.06) = ₹24.4 crore ÷ 0.065 = about ₹375 crore. Compare that with about ₹322 crore at 5% growth. One percentage point added roughly ₹53 crore to a figure standing at the end of year five, before discounting.

children.text: How High Can Growth Go? Not As High As You Think
A company growing forever at a rate above the economy eventually becomes larger than the economy. That is the discipline on this assumption, and it is arithmetic, not opinion.

stats.label: India nominal GDP growth
stats.context: FY26 estimate, with 10.3% recorded in the first quarter of FY27

stats.label: Sensible terminal growth
stats.context: Nominal, for a mature Indian business, and always below long-run nominal GDP growth

body.text: Two hard rules. First, terminal growth must be below the cost of capital, or the formula produces a negative or infinite answer and the model is meaningless. Second, it must be below long-run nominal growth for the economy, because rupee cash flows growing faster than nominal GDP forever means the company eats the whole country. If someone defends 9% terminal growth, ask them what share of Indian GDP the company holds in the year 2075.

body.title: When the formula breaks
body.question: An analyst builds a model with a cost of capital of 12.5% and a terminal growth rate of 13%. What happens?
options: The terminal value is very large but still usable with caution
The denominator turns negative, so the terminal value comes out negative and the model is meaningless
The model automatically switches to an exit multiple
Nothing unusual, because growth above the discount rate is common for fast growing companies
body.explanation: WACC minus g becomes 12.5% minus 13%, which is minus 0.5%, so the formula returns a negative terminal value for a profitable business. The formula assumes growth continues forever, and nothing can grow forever faster than the rate at which its cash is discounted. As g approaches WACC from below, the value explodes towards infinity, which is equally useless. Terminal growth must sit well below the cost of capital.

children.text: Cross-Check One: What Multiple Does Your Growth Imply?
Take the base case terminal value of ₹321.8 crore and divide it by final year EBITDA of ₹64.4 crore. That is an implied exit multiple of about 5 times EBITDA.

body.title: Compute the implied exit multiple
body.prompt: A terminal value of ₹322 crore is calculated for a company whose final forecast year EBITDA is ₹64.4 crore. What EV/EBITDA multiple does that terminal value imply? Answer to one decimal place.
body.explanation: ₹322 crore ÷ ₹64.4 crore = about 5.0 times. Now ask whether a buyer in year five would really pay only 5 times EBITDA for a business of this kind. If comparable tile makers trade at 8 or 9 times, this terminal value may be conservative rather than aggressive, and the DCF is understating the company.

children.text: Cross-Check Two: What Growth Does Your Multiple Imply?

Run it the other way. Suppose you use the exit multiple method instead, at 8 times final year EBITDA. Terminal value becomes ₹515.4 crore, enterprise value rises to about ₹352.7 crore and equity value to about ₹292.7 crore after ₹60 crore of net debt.

body.caption: Rearranging the perpetuity formula to find the growth rate an exit multiple implies

children.text: Feed the numbers in and that 8 times multiple implies perpetual growth of about 7.7%. That is close to India's nominal GDP growth rate, sustained forever, by a regional tile manufacturer. State it that way in a meeting and the assumption defends itself or collapses, which is exactly what you want.

body.title: The same company, two terminal value methods

columns.label: Perpetuity growth at 5%
points: Implied exit multiple about 5 times EBITDA
Defensible on growth, possibly conservative on the multiple

columns.label: Exit multiple at 8 times EBITDA
points: Defensible on the multiple, hard to defend on growth

body.text: The gap between those two answers is the honest range for this business. A valuer who shows both, explains the implied figures and presents a range is doing the job. One who picks whichever method produces the number the client wanted is doing something else.

children.text: The Assumption Hiding Behind the Growth Rate

body.title: Growth is not free, even in perpetuity

children.text: Lesson 2.2 established that growth needs reinvestment equal to g divided by ROIC. That rule does not stop applying after year five. A terminal value that assumes 5% growth forever while the company reinvests nothing is assuming growth out of thin air.

content.caption: The value driver version, which makes the reinvestment explicit

children.text: Konkan's final year operating profit after tax is about ₹33.8 crore. Assume it earns 15% on invested capital in the long run, so sustaining 5% growth requires reinvesting a third of its profit. The terminal value works out to about ₹316 crore, against ₹321.8 crore from the simple formula. The two are close here, which is a sign the simple version is not smuggling in free growth.
Run this check whenever the simple formula gives a terminal value far above the value driver version. The gap is usually growth that nobody is paying for.

content.text: In the very long run, competition drags returns on capital down towards the cost of capital. A model assuming a company earns 25% on capital forever is assuming its moat never erodes. Assuming returns fade towards the cost of capital over time is more honest, and it lowers the terminal value.

children.text: Six Ways Terminal Value Goes Wrong

body.caption: What to check, and what it does to the answer

cells: Final year cash flow is abnormal
A year with unusually low capital expenditure inflates the base for the whole perpetuity
Normalise the final year: capital expenditure should roughly equal depreciation in a steady state
Terminal year sits at a cyclical peak
Peak margins are capitalised forever
Use mid-cycle margins for the terminal year in cyclical sectors such as cement, steel and real estate
Growth rate above long-run nominal GDP growth
The company outgrows the economy forever
Cap terminal growth below nominal GDP growth, usually 4% to 6% in India
Growth close to the cost of capital
The denominator shrinks and the value explodes
Keep a wide gap, and show the sensitivity grid
Terminal value not discounted
The whole figure is overstated by the year five discount factor, here about 45%
Multiply the terminal value by the final year discount factor
No cross-check against a multiple
The implied exit multiple is absurd and nobody notices
Always divide the terminal value by final year EBITDA and sanity check it

body.title: Ninety one percent
body.scenario: A model supporting a ₹900 crore acquisition of a speciality chemicals business shows an enterprise value of ₹920 crore, of which ₹837 crore, or 91%, is terminal value. The forecast runs ten years. Terminal growth is 6.5% against a WACC of 11%. In the terminal year, capital expenditure is 2% of revenue while depreciation is 5.5%, and EBITDA margin is 24% against a ten year historical average of 17%.
body.prompt: Set out your assessment for the investment committee.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Ninety one percent of the value sits beyond the forecast, and the forecast is already ten years long. In effect we are paying ₹900 crore for a set of assumptions about the years after 2036. That alone justifies rejecting the model in its present form.
2. The denominator is 4.5 percentage points, which is thin. At a more conventional 5% growth the terminal value falls sharply. I would ask for the full sensitivity grid across WACC from 11% to 13% and growth from 4% to 6%.
3. The terminal year is not a steady state. Capital expenditure at 2% of revenue against 5.5% depreciation means the model assumes the plant shrinks forever while cash flow stays high. In perpetuity, capital expenditure should roughly match depreciation. Fixing that alone cuts the terminal cash flow base materially.
4. The terminal margin of 24% against a 17% ten year average capitalises the best margin the business has ever seen, forever. For a cyclical chemicals business, a mid-cycle margin is the right basis.
5. Cross-check the terminal value against a multiple. Divide ₹837 crore by terminal year EBITDA and compare with what listed speciality chemicals companies trade at. If the implied multiple is above the sector, the model is buying at a premium to today's market and calling it intrinsic value.
6. My recommendation: rerun with a normalised terminal year, mid-cycle margins, growth at 5% and the sensitivity grid attached. If the deal only works on the current assumptions, the price is wrong, not the model.

body.title: The upper bound
body.textWithBlank: The terminal growth rate must stay below the long-run ___ growth rate of the economy, or the company eventually becomes larger than the economy itself.
body.explanation: India's nominal GDP growth was estimated at about 8.6% for FY26. A terminal growth assumption of 4% to 6% sits sensibly below that. Anything at or above it is a claim about the company taking over the economy.

body.title: Interrogate any terminal value
steps: Compute terminal value as a percentage of enterprise value, and say it out loud
Check that terminal growth is below both the cost of capital and long-run nominal GDP growth
Confirm the final forecast year is normal: mid-cycle margins, capital expenditure roughly equal to depreciation
Divide terminal value by final year EBITDA and test the implied exit multiple against comparable companies
If an exit multiple was used, back out the growth rate it implies
Verify the terminal value has actually been discounted by the final year factor
Ask whether the assumed return on capital can survive competition for that long
Present the whole thing as a grid across growth and discount rate, never as one number

body.label: MOSPI: national accounts and GDP estimates
body.description: The official source for Indian GDP data, real and nominal. Check the latest nominal growth figure before you accept any terminal growth assumption in a valuation report.

cards.definition: The value of all cash flows beyond the explicit forecast, captured in one figure at the end of the forecast.
Final year cash flow grown by g and divided by the cost of capital less g.
Final year EBITDA multiplied by an assumed sale multiple.
Terminal value divided by final year EBITDA, used to sanity check a growth assumption.
The perpetual growth an assumed exit multiple works out to.
A terminal year with normal margins and capital expenditure roughly equal to depreciation.
The assumption that returns on capital decline towards the cost of capital as competition catches up.

points: Terminal value was about 73% of Konkan Ceramics' enterprise value, which is normal and is why it deserves more scrutiny than the forecast years.
Moving terminal growth from 3% to 7% moved enterprise value from about ₹205 crore to about ₹315 crore.
Terminal growth must be below the cost of capital, or the formula returns nonsense, and below long-run nominal GDP growth, which was estimated at about 8.6% for FY26.
Cross-check both ways: 5% growth implied an exit multiple of about 5 times, while an 8 times exit multiple implied about 7.7% perpetual growth.
The final forecast year must be a steady state, with mid-cycle margins and capital expenditure roughly equal to depreciation.
Growth still needs reinvestment after year five. The value driver version of the formula makes that explicit and stops free growth creeping in.
Present terminal value as a range with its assumptions visible, never as a single confident figure.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Konkan Ceramics and the chemicals target are fictional. GDP figures are official estimates as at September 2026 and are revised regularly. Terminal value conventions differ between valuers, and any valuation used in a transaction or filing should be prepared by a qualified professional.
